ui.d_title: {name} Cost of Living & Quality of Life: Six Scores, Ranked {trank} of 55
ui.d_desc: {name} sits at {tot} on our six-dimension livability score, rank {trank} of 55 countries. Strongest dimension: {best} ({best_s}); weakest: {worst} ({worst_s}). Includes 12 World Bank indicators with source years, one-bedroom rents for three cities and the main visa routes.
ui.d_h1: Living in {name}: where the six dimensions hold up and where they don't
ui.d_lede: Weighting all six dimensions equally puts {name} at {tot}, rank {trank} of {n} candidate countries. The strongest dimension is {best} ({best_s}, rank {best_rank}); the soft spot is {worst} ({worst_s}, rank {worst_rank}). Every figure below carries its World Bank source value, year and percentile position.
ui.note_dims: How to read the score: each dimension converts your rank among the 55 candidates into a 0-100 percentile. Above 70 is a genuine strength, around 50 is mid-pack, below 40 means the country is clearly behind its peer group at that dimension.
ui.btn_test: Find the country that fits me
ui.text_best: {fact}. That is rank {rank} across the {n} countries reporting this indicator, and it is the main source of {name}'s overall score.
ui.text_worst: {fact}. It ranks {rank} here, so this is the trade-off you accept when you pick {name}.
ui.ad1: Advertisement · city rents and visa routes below
ui.sec_city: City cost of living: one-bedroom rent, mid-market
ui.note_city: Rents are mid-range asking prices for a central one-bedroom flat, grouped into three bands so you can feel the gap between cities. They are not official statistics and exclude utilities and deposits.
ui.note_visa: The above is an editorial summary of common routes, not legal advice. Check the latest published requirements, quotas and processing times with each country's immigration authority.
ui.tbl_src: Source: World Bank Open Data API (CC BY 4.0). Latest available year per country, used as published — no estimates, interpolation or backfilling, and missing values stay missing. Percentiles show relative position among the candidates, not an international rating.
ui.sec_peer: How it compares with nearby countries
ui.note_peer: Scores are the six-dimension equal-weight average. For a full single-dimension ordering go to the rankings; to weight the dimensions your own way, take the 18-question test and rebuild the score with the sliders.
ui.note_pairs: Each comparison page puts two countries' six dimension scores and all 12 World Bank indicators, with years, into one row-by-row table, then works out what the cost and income gap actually amounts to.
ui.foot_share_note: Anyone you share it with opens the same public data page; no personal information is attached.
ui.foot_disc: Disclaimer: this page summarises public statistics and is not immigration, legal or tax advice. Any relocation, visa or tax arrangement should be discussed with a licensed professional.
ui.foot_src: Data source: World Bank Open Data (CC BY 4.0), with the year given for every indicator. City rents and visa tags are editorial estimates, not official data. Updated: {updated}
ui.foot_copy: MBTI · Life Geography / Where To Live
ui.ds_desc: The latest available values and years for {name} across 12 indicators: price level index, GDP per capita (PPP), life expectancy, homicide rate, PM2.5, forest area, population density, female labour participation, health spending as a share of GDP, internet use, unemployment and urbanisation.
ui.faq_q1: Where does {name} rank overall among the 55 countries?
ui.faq_a1: With all six dimensions weighted equally, {name} scores {tot} and ranks {trank} of {n}. {best} comes in at {best_s} ({best_word}, rank {best_rank}) and {worst} at {worst_s} ({worst_word}, rank {worst_rank}). These are percentiles of the candidate set, not absolute verdicts.
ui.faq_q2: How expensive is {name}, and what do people earn there?
ui.faq_a2: {price}; {gdp}. Both are macro averages: the price level index compares PPP conversion factors with market exchange rates and ignores individual spending patterns, while GDP per capita in PPP terms measures output rather than take-home pay.
ui.faq_q3: Can the data alone tell me whether to move to {name}?
ui.faq_a3: No. These are national statistical averages and cannot capture differences between cities and neighbourhoods, visa and tax rules, language and access to public services, or your own profession and family situation. Use them for shortlisting and cross-country comparison, and consult a licensed professional for the actual move, visa and tax arrangements.
ui.idx_title: Cost of Living & Quality of Life in 55 Countries: Scores, Ranks, 12 Indicators
ui.idx_desc: A single table of living conditions across 55 countries: overall livability score, six dimension scores, region and the year behind each World Bank indicator, sorted by overall score. Click any header to re-sort, or open a country for the full breakdown.
ui.idx_h1: Living conditions in 55 countries and regions
ui.idx_lede: The overall score is the equal-weight average of six dimensions, so it only shows where a country sits at the default weighting. Your own ranking depends on what you care about — answer 18 questions on the test page to recalculate with your weights, or open a country page for raw indicators and years.
ui.idx_note: Click a column header to sort. Scores are percentiles (0-100) within the 55 countries; "—" means the World Bank does not publish that indicator for the country.

USA.name: United States
USA.visa_note: Most work visas go through a lottery and stay tied to one employer, and green-card backlogs swing wildly by country of birth and category.
USA.hook: The earning ceiling is the highest in this set, but health cover and schooling are the hidden line items.
USA.tip: Compare state income tax and insurance deductibles before you compare rent.

CAN.name: Canada
CAN.visa_note: Selection is points-based, rewarding language scores and Canadian credentials, and cut-off scores have been climbing.
CAN.hook: The immigration pathway is unusually legible; housing costs and winter are what you pay for that clarity.
CAN.tip: Budget winter heating and car insurance as fixed monthly costs, not seasonal extras.

GBR.name: United Kingdom
GBR.visa_note: A licensed sponsor and a salary floor are both mandatory, and the rules have been tightened several times in recent years.
GBR.hook: London and the northern cities behave like two different countries on cost of living.
GBR.tip: Outside London, income left after rent is often higher than inside it.

IRL.name: Ireland
IRL.visa_note: The Critical Skills occupation list decides how fast you are processed, and Dublin's rental market is brutally competitive.
IRL.hook: An English-speaking foothold inside the EU single market, with rent as the price of admission.
IRL.tip: Secure long-term housing before signing the job contract.

DEU.name: Germany
DEU.visa_note: The Blue Card carries a minimum salary threshold and foreign degrees need Anabin recognition; German pays off for permanent residence.
DEU.hook: Engineering and manufacturing demand run deep, and rent regulation genuinely protects tenants.
DEU.tip: Look at warm rent rather than cold rent: utilities are the part that surprises people.

FRA.name: France
FRA.visa_note: Passeport Talent covers research, company founding and high-salary roles, though administrative processing is slow.
FRA.hook: Public healthcare and childcare support are excellent; taxes and social contributions take a visible bite.
FRA.tip: Compare countries on net pay after social contributions, never on gross salary.

NLD.name: Netherlands
NLD.visa_note: Salary thresholds scale with age, and your employer has to be a recognised sponsor.
NLD.hook: English works as a working language almost everywhere, but the housing shortage is national rather than local.
NLD.tip: Either accept the social-housing queue or budget for expensive private rent.

BEL.name: Belgium
BEL.visa_note: Regionalised administration means Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels each run the process their own way.
BEL.hook: EU institutions concentrate here, so commuting and a multilingual daily life are the default.
BEL.tip: Confirm the working language: Dutch-speaking and French-speaking regions are different worlds.

CHE.name: Switzerland
CHE.visa_note: Non-EU nationals are capped by annual quotas, so an employer offer has to arrive first.
CHE.hook: Salaries are Europe's highest and prices match, yet net savings usually still beat the neighbours.
CHE.tip: Carry mandatory health insurance premiums as a separate budget line.

AUT.name: Austria
AUT.visa_note: The Red-White-Red Card scores qualifications and shortage occupations, with basic German earning extra points.
AUT.hook: Vienna's social housing keeps living costs well below what the salary levels would suggest.
AUT.tip: Applying for a municipal flat early can cut rent dramatically.

SWE.name: Sweden
SWE.visa_note: Permits are tied to the employer and must meet the collective-agreement wage for the sector.
SWE.hook: Work-life balance is the headline; winter darkness is the cost line nobody quotes.
SWE.tip: Put winter travel and vitamin D in the budget and take the darkness seriously.

NOR.name: Norway
NOR.visa_note: Pay must match Norwegian norms, and non-EU applications are screened closely.
NOR.hook: Oil, gas and marine industries pay well; groceries and alcohol sit at the top of the European range.
NOR.tip: Round the food and alcohol budget up — that is where the surprises come from.

DNK.name: Denmark
DNK.visa_note: The Positive List follows shortage occupations, and language and integration requirements keep ratcheting up.
DNK.hook: Cycling infrastructure and high social trust are the everyday experience you are buying.
DNK.tip: Treat cycling distance as a housing variable, not a lifestyle preference.

FIN.name: Finland
FIN.visa_note: The specialist route moves quickly; the startup visa needs a positive evaluation from an approved assessor.
FIN.hook: Education and tech ecosystems are stable, and the winter is genuinely long.
FIN.tip: When viewing flats, check heating and ventilation — they decide how winter feels.

ISL.name: Iceland
ISL.visa_note: Roles must be advertised on the local market first, and non-EU processing is slow.
ISL.hook: A small population means tight networks and an extremely thin rental market.
ISL.tip: Popular areas rent through contacts, so start looking two months ahead.

PRT.name: Portugal
PRT.visa_note: D7 and D8 are generous towards remote and passive income, with light physical-presence rules.
PRT.hook: Western Europe's cost floor, though rents in the popular cities have climbed hard.
PRT.tip: Staying outside the tourist core typically saves about 30% on rent.

ESP.name: Spain
ESP.visa_note: The nomad visa ties income to a multiple of the local minimum wage, and processing varies by region.
ESP.hook: Climate and daily rhythm are the draw; youth unemployment is the persistent asterisk.
ESP.tip: Pick the industry before the city — the sector matters more than the map.

ITA.name: Italy
ITA.visa_note: Bureaucracy is layered, and language plus local variation shape how the first year actually feels.
ITA.hook: The north-south gap is wide: the south is cheap but thin on jobs.
ITA.tip: Double your estimate for administrative timelines and never plan around a fixed date.

GRC.name: Greece
GRC.visa_note: Golden visa thresholds were raised and are now priced by region, so check the current tier before you commit.
GRC.hook: Low living costs and plenty of coastline, with a weak earning side.
GRC.tip: Winter heating and island ferry fares belong in the monthly budget.

POL.name: Poland
POL.visa_note: Work permits require a labour-market test, though shortage roles such as IT clear quickly.
POL.hook: Central Europe's fastest growth at a cost level still well under Western Europe.
POL.tip: Check the contract type: B2B and employment contracts carry very different tax loads.

CZE.name: Czechia
CZE.visa_note: The Employee Card needs an employer and a labour-office step, and Prague's housing is tight.
CZE.hook: Manufacturing and game studios cluster here, and beer is cheaper than water.
CZE.tip: Two metro stops out of the centre can change rent by 40%.

EST.name: Estonia
EST.visa_note: Public services are digital to the core; the startup visa requires a committee review.
EST.hook: e-Residency and a dense startup scene, offset by almost no winter daylight.
EST.tip: The nomad visa has an income floor — verify the current threshold before applying.

HUN.name: Hungary
HUN.visa_note: Policy has tightened recently, and guest-worker categories plus family reunification rules change often.
HUN.hook: Low costs and strong thermal-bath and medical tourism, with a forint that swings.
HUN.tip: If you budget in euros, keep a currency buffer in the calculation.

ROU.name: Romania
ROU.visa_note: Work permits are subject to annual quotas, and IT and outsourcing roles are the easiest entry.
ROU.hook: Very low costs and excellent internet, with public services that vary street by street.
ROU.tip: Confirm what your health insurance actually covers before you arrive.

TUR.name: Turkey
TUR.visa_note: Short-term residence renewals need proof of stable income, and lira depreciation feeds straight into local prices.
TUR.hook: A bridge between Europe and Asia at friendly prices, with inflation as the standing pressure.
TUR.tip: Annual rent paid upfront is common — agree the payment structure in writing.

JPN.name: Japan
JPN.visa_note: The points-based highly skilled route earns preferential treatment; the Business Manager visa needs a real operation and capital.
JPN.hook: Order and public services are first class; the language is the wall most newcomers hit.
JPN.tip: Treat commute time as a core living cost rather than a detail.

CHN.name: China
CHN.visa_note: Work permit and residence permit are two separate steps, and enforcement details differ from city to city.
CHN.hook: Megacities concentrate opportunity, while hukou and social-insurance rules vary sharply.
CHN.tip: Confirm where social insurance is paid — it drives your long-term entitlements.

KOR.name: South Korea
KOR.visa_note: Employment visas need an employer sponsor, and long-term residence adds points and language requirements.
KOR.hook: Digital infrastructure and medical efficiency run high, and the deposit-based rental system is unique.
KOR.tip: Jeonse and monthly rent create completely different cash-flow pressure.

SGP.name: Singapore
SGP.visa_note: EP runs on the COMPASS points framework, with finance and tech roles concentrated in the CBD.
SGP.hook: Efficiency and safety are exceptional; housing and car ownership are the expensive parts.
SGP.tip: HDB and private condo prices differ enormously — read the lease type before signing.

MYS.name: Malaysia
MYS.visa_note: MM2H thresholds have changed repeatedly, so verify current fixed-deposit and income requirements.
MYS.hook: English works everywhere and costs are low, though public transport thins out beyond the core.
MYS.tip: If you settle in the suburbs, budget for a car and tolls.

THA.name: Thailand
THA.visa_note: The DTV targets remote work and soft-power activities, and any local work still needs a separate permit.
THA.hook: Low costs and easy services, with visa rules that change more often than the weather.
THA.tip: Mind the boundary between a work permit and remote work for foreign clients.

VNM.name: Vietnam
VNM.visa_note: Work permits require matching qualifications and role descriptions, and processing is administrative.
VNM.hook: Fast growth at low cost, with urban noise and traffic you simply have to adapt to.
VNM.tip: Sign a long lease directly with the landlord to avoid sublet chains.

IDN.name: Indonesia
IDN.visa_note: Second Home needs proof of funds, and work permits are tied to a ratio of local hires.
IDN.hook: Islands differ wildly — Bali now prices close to a mid-size city.
IDN.tip: Choose the island before the city; cost baselines are not comparable across islands.

PHL.name: Philippines
PHL.visa_note: Work visas need a labour department permit, and the retirement visa sets deposit thresholds by age.
PHL.hook: English is widely spoken, alongside infrastructure gaps and typhoon season.
PHL.tip: Plan for typhoon season and power outages as recurring conditions, not exceptions.

HKG.name: Hong Kong SAR
HKG.visa_note: TTPS is banded by salary or a top-university degree, and renewals are tied to employment.
HKG.hook: Low taxes and fast administration, with floor area as the compromise you make.
HKG.tip: Compare price per square metre, not the headline rent.

AUS.name: Australia
AUS.visa_note: Independent skilled migration invites by EOI points and occupation lists, and the points competition is fierce.
AUS.hook: Climate and outdoor access are strong, and regional sponsorship can be the cheaper route to status.
AUS.tip: Regional nomination can cut the points you need substantially.

NZL.name: New Zealand
NZL.visa_note: Green List occupations go straight to residence; everything else must clear the median wage line.
NZL.hook: Few people and nature close by, with a limited total number of roles and salary ceilings.
NZL.tip: Weigh job density ahead of scenery when you choose where to live.

MEX.name: Mexico
MEX.visa_note: Temporary residence can be applied for on savings or income, and paid work needs a separate permit.
MEX.hook: North America's cost floor, with safety varying sharply from block to block.
MEX.tip: Choose neighbourhoods on safety data, not on city averages.

CRI.name: Costa Rica
CRI.visa_note: Retiree and investor routes need stable income or a set investment, and the nomad visa has an income floor.
CRI.hook: Healthcare and eco-tourism are mature, and prices run above the neighbouring countries.
CRI.tip: Budget private health cover separately from the public system.

PAN.name: Panama
PAN.visa_note: Friendly Nations works off a nationality list, and the pensioner route needs a lifetime annuity.
PAN.hook: A dollarised economy with finance concentrated in the capital and a sharp urban-rural split.
PAN.tip: Dollar pricing means no currency buffer — plan in dollars throughout.

COL.name: Colombia
COL.visa_note: The nomad visa has an income threshold, and work visas stay tightly bound to one employer.
COL.hook: Climate is set by altitude, costs are low, and safety has to be judged area by area.
COL.tip: Altitude decides climate here — pick the elevation before the city.

CHL.name: Chile
CHL.visa_note: Work visas need a local contract, and investment routes carry minimum amounts.
CHL.hook: The steadiest governance in South America, at prices above its neighbours.
CHL.tip: Winter air pollution is noticeable in the central-southern cities.

ARG.name: Argentina
ARG.visa_note: Rental-income residence requires proof of stable passive income, and exchange controls shift constantly.
ARG.hook: Culture and quality of daily life are high, while inflation keeps rewriting the budget.
ARG.tip: Keep your books in dollars or euros to avoid local-currency illusion.

BRA.name: Brazil
BRA.visa_note: The nomad visa needs monthly income proof, and work visas are tied to the employer.
BRA.hook: Huge and internally varied, with safety that has to be assessed neighbourhood by neighbourhood.
BRA.tip: In São Paulo, commuting time and security are the hidden costs.

URY.name: Uruguay
URY.visa_note: Residence routes are relatively stable, with steady income as the main qualifier.
URY.hook: Institutionally calm for Latin America with a slow rhythm, at prices on the high side.
URY.tip: Low-season and high-season rents diverge sharply — negotiate the terms.

PER.name: Peru
PER.visa_note: Work visas need an employer sponsor, and the retirement visa has an annuity requirement.
PER.hook: Excellent food at low cost, with a coastal fog season that wears on mood.
PER.tip: In Lima, pick the district first — seafront districts cost noticeably more.

ARE.name: United Arab Emirates
ARE.visa_note: Golden visas target investors, specialised talent and top students, and personal tax is minimal.
ARE.hook: Zero personal income tax, paid for with summer heat and no permanent-residence track.
ARE.tip: Add summer electricity and air-conditioning servicing to monthly costs.

ISR.name: Israel
ISR.visa_note: Standard work visas are screened strictly, and long-term status pathways are narrow.
ISR.hook: High-tech density and high costs, with the security situation as the variable you cannot model.
ISR.tip: Treat proximity to a shelter as a hard requirement when choosing housing.

ZAF.name: South Africa
ZAF.visa_note: The critical-skills list drives approvals, and long-term status is tied to employment.
ZAF.hook: Nature and low costs, with power supply and personal safety as daily variables.
ZAF.tip: Budget for backup power and private security from day one.

GEO.name: Georgia
GEO.visa_note: Many nationalities can stay a year visa-free, though work and business activity have separate registration rules.
GEO.hook: Low costs and a low threshold to entry, with limited earning opportunities.
GEO.tip: Great for freelancers, but you have to arrange your own health cover.

SRB.name: Serbia
SRB.visa_note: Business and self-employment routes need a local company or evidence of activity; nomad residence has a time limit.
SRB.hook: A European cost floor with an active IT and outsourcing market.
SRB.tip: Check renewal and tax treatment for long-term residence early.

HRV.name: Croatia
HRV.visa_note: Nomad residence is issued yearly and requires health insurance plus proof of accommodation.
HRV.hook: Superb coastline, with rents that spike hard in the tourist season.
HRV.tip: On the coast, rent annually rather than by peak-season month.

MAR.name: Morocco
MAR.visa_note: Long stays require a residence card, and work permits are tied to a local employer.
MAR.hook: Where Europe meets Africa at low cost, with an administration that moves slowly.
MAR.tip: French or Arabic ability visibly changes how smoothly paperwork goes.

EGY.name: Egypt
EGY.visa_note: Currency controls and exchange-rate swings affect moving money in and out, so check the current rules.
EGY.hook: Extremely low costs, with public services and air quality varying widely.
EGY.tip: If you convert from dollars, price in the risk of currency controls.

IND.name: India
IND.visa_note: Employment visas need a local employer and labour clearance, and long-term status options are narrow.
IND.hook: A deep IT and startup ecosystem sitting on infrastructure that varies enormously.
IND.tip: Choose housing by commute radius — travel time is a real cost here.
